text:
"RAG's dead" is the wrong conclusion to a valid observation.

It's not dead. It's just being forced into jobs it wasn't built for.

The "embed everything" era's ending.

Semantic search is often the wrong tool for technical data.

---

Cursor vs. Claude Code highlights this split perfectly.

Cursor relies on permanent embeddings so the agent always knows the map.

It's fast and seamless.

But it's expensive to maintain and introduces semantic noise.

Approximations can mislead.

---

Claude Code uses grep and glob instead.

No permanent index. No wasted tokens embedding files you'll never query.

It searches for exact patterns, not just "similar" concepts.

In a codebase, exactness matters more than similarity.

---

Semantic search's a blunt instrument for technical tasks.

If you need a specific function definition, you don't want a "top 5 most similar" list.

You want the line number.

Grep gives you the truth. Embeddings give you a guess.

---

Modern retrieval layers need multiple tools.

I use grep for code navigation and BM25 for keyword search.

I only embed high-level documentation.

Data type determines the tool, not the other way around.

---

Context windows are massive, but noise's still the bottleneck.

Feeding an agent 10 "relevant" snippets via RAG often creates more confusion than one exact match from a regex search.

Efficiency isn't about cost. It's about cognitive load.

---

RAG isn't dead. It's finally being used correctly.

It's one tool in a larger retrieval stack, not the whole stack.

Choosing the wrong one's a logic error.

Your agent's only as smart as the context you provide.

---

How're you drawing the line between tools and cognitive logic in your stack?

#AIEngineering #LLMs #RAG #ClaudeCode
idea_source: RAGs are dead — that's what a colleague said the other day. It stuck with me because RAG is one of the pillars of data engineering. But he was right, in a specific context. He was explaining how Cursor works vs Claude Code: Cursor uses permanent embeddings so the agent always knows where everything is, updated constantly as new code is generated. Fast, efficient. But pricey and creates noise in the data. Claude Code, on the other hand, uses grep and glob — regex-based search to find exactly what's needed. No wasted tokens embedding things you never query. Exact matches, not approximations. Approximations can mislead. The deeper insight: RAGs were born out of necessity — to give LLMs better context. But they lack direction. New tools fill the gaps where RAGs are inefficient and costly. Today I use grep and glob for specific code navigation, BM25 for keyword search, and I only embed what actually needs semantic search — large documentation, not everything. The question engineers should ask: what kind of data are you dealing with? That determines the tool. RAG is not dead. It's just finally being used correctly.
